Abkhazia.text: Abkhazia’s foreign ministry connects the alternating green and white stripes to the Mountain Republic of 1918. It describes green as life and white as a bright future.
Abkhazia.scope: Source's own interpretation; status of the entity is disputed.

Afghanistan.text: The Afghanistan Analysts Network describes the Taliban’s white flag with the Islamic profession of faith. It does not establish why white was chosen.
Afghanistan.scope: The CSV identifies the de facto Islamic Emirate flag; other Afghan flags remain in use. The color’s origin is unresolved here.

Cook Islands.text: The Cook Islands Constitution describes blue as representing the Pacific Ocean in which the islands are scattered.
Cook Islands.scope: The constitution's account of the blue field; it does not supply an origin for every color here.

Czechia.text: Prague Castle traces the national flag’s colors to the same heraldic basis as the historic coats of arms of the lands.
Czechia.scope: Broad historical origin; the source does not assign a separate meaning to each color.

Northern Cyprus.text: The red-and-white design reverses the colors of the Turkish flag and adds two red stripes; accounts differ on the symbolism of those stripes.
Northern Cyprus.source_name: Ryan D. Griffiths, Secession and the Sovereignty Game, chapter 9
Northern Cyprus.scope: An academic account of the design; status of the entity is disputed. The chapter may require access.

Palestine.text: The Palestinian foreign ministry presents a commonly cited account linking the colors to Arab nationalist ideas and the Arab Revolt flag; it also discusses other interpretations.
Palestine.scope: Attributed account; the source itself describes multiple versions of the colors' origins.

Somaliland.text: Somaliland’s constitution specifies green, white and red bands, a white inscription and a black star. This description does not explain why the colors were selected.
Somaliland.scope: Color origins remain unresolved; status of the entity is disputed.

South Ossetia.text: The South Ossetian foreign ministry describes white, red and yellow as a traditional Ossetian palette and associates them with wisdom, courage and prosperity, respectively.
South Ossetia.source_name: South Ossetia Ministry of Foreign Affairs
South Ossetia.scope: The authority's interpretation; status of the entity is disputed.

Transnistria.text: A local travel source describes the red-green-red flag as closely resembling the former Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic flag.
Transnistria.scope: This explains a design connection, not why the original colors were chosen; status of the entity is disputed.

Western Sahara (Sahrawi Arab Democratic.text: Flags of the World describes the flag as using pan-Arab colors and as resembling the Palestinian flag, with a crescent and star added.
Western Sahara (Sahrawi Arab Democratic.source_name: Flags of the World, Western Sahara
Western Sahara (Sahrawi Arab Democratic.scope: A vexillological account, with alternative interpretations on the linked page; sovereignty is disputed.

Spain.text: The Spanish royal household explains that Charles III commissioned a more readily distinguishable naval ensign in 1785. The red-yellow-red design later became the national flag.
Spain.source_name: Spanish Royal Household, Symbols of State
Spain.scope: Purpose and origin of the design; this source does not assign a separate symbolic meaning to each color.
